crops.wild: Wild einkorn (Triticum monococcum subsp. aegilopoides, syn. T. boeoticum)
crops.wl: Short grass under 70 cm, not very productive; ripe ears shatter and drop their kernels, which sit in tough husks (glumes).
crops.ch: Ear stays intact when ripe (non-shattering), so it can be reaped; slightly larger kernels. Self-pollination helped keep the new traits.
crops.ce: Karaca Dağ, SE Turkey (DNA fingerprinting)
crops.cn: Wild einkorn gathered at Abu Hureyra (c. 10,700–9000 BC) and Mureybet (c. 9800–9300 BC); wheat cultivation in the Fertile Crescent from c. 9600 BC
crops.dn: Domestic form after c. 8800 BC at Çayönü, Cafer Höyük and possibly Nevalı Çori; genetics also suggest several domestications
sp: Einkorn introduced to Cyprus c. 7500 BC
Wheats reach Britain and Scandinavia by 4000 BC
Declines in favour of emmer from c. 2000 BCE
crops.today: A niche hulled wheat; contains gluten and more protein than modern red wheats.
crops.fact: Models once claimed domestication could take 20–200 years; archaeology shows over a thousand years of pre-domestication cultivation.

crops.wild: Wild emmer (Triticum turgidum subsp. dicoccoides), itself a hybrid of wild Triticum urartu × goatgrass Aegilops speltoides
crops.wl: Grass 50–70 cm with 10–15 cm awned ears that shatter when ripe; spikelets drill into the soil with their awns; chaff hard to remove.
crops.ch: Ears no longer shatter, so whole spikelets can be harvested (hulled emmer); later free-threshing forms whose grains fall free when threshed.
crops.ce: Çayönü, SE Anatolia (genetics: domesticated once in SE Anatolia)
crops.cn: Wild emmer first cultivated in the southern Levant as early as 9600 BC; wild grains at Netiv HaGdud (PPNA)
crops.dn: Çayönü c. 8300–7600 BC: spikelet scars of a hulled domestic type; Tell Aswad c. 8500–8200 BC claimed (less reliable grain-size method); location still debated
sp: Introduced to Cyprus as early as 8600 BC
Shortly after 6000 BC; later main Pharaonic wheat
Reaches Germany and Spain by 5000 BC
crops.today: Still grown; one of the three grains sold as farro in Italy.
crops.fact: Emmer was the main wheat of Pharaonic Egypt; with barley it was the basis of Egyptian bread and beer.

crops.wild: No wild ancestor: hybrid of a domesticated tetraploid (emmer-type) wheat × Tausch's goatgrass (Aegilops tauschii)
crops.wl: The goatgrass parent is a wild annual grass of the Caucasus, Caspian and Central Asia; it gave wheat its D genome.
crops.ch: Six chromosome sets (four from emmer, two from goatgrass), free-threshing grain; 20th-century dwarfing genes (Norin 10) powered the Green Revolution.
crops.ce: South Caucasus / south-west Caspian area
crops.cn: Arose spontaneously in farmers' fields of already-domesticated wheat
crops.dn: Originated c. 8,000 years ago; oldest hexaploid wheat DNA from Çatalhöyük seeds, c. 6400–6200 BC
sp: Wheat cultivated in India around 3500 BC
Juan Garrido sows first wheat in New Spain, 1520s
Prairie colonisation makes North America a grain exporter
crops.today: ~95% of all wheat; wheat (799 Mt, 2024) covers more land than any food crop.
crops.fact: World trade in wheat is greater than that of all other crops combined.

crops.wild: Wild barley (Hordeum vulgare subsp. spontaneum)
crops.wl: Two-rowed ear with hulled grains and a brittle spike that falls apart when ripe; ground into flour at Ohalo II 23,000 years ago.
crops.ch: Non-brittle ear (Bt1/Bt2 mutations), then naked (hulless) and six-rowed forms with three fertile spikelets per node; grains became rounder.
crops.ce: Tell Aswad, Syria (earliest domestic two-row barley)
crops.cn: Gilgal I granary of thousands of wild barley grains, c. 11,700–10,550 years ago: cultivation before domestication
crops.dn: Domestic two-row barley at Tell Aswad, c. 10,200–9,550 years ago; Jarmo 9000–7000 BC; Tibet and Ethiopia possibly extra centres (debated)
sp: Domesticated barley reaches eastern Finland by 4200 BC
Grown since Early Mumun period, c. 1500–850 BC
Staple of Tibetan cuisine since the 5th century AD
crops.today: Fourth grain by quantity (146 Mt, 2023); 70% feeds animals, 30% beer, whisky, food.
crops.fact: Barley beer was probably one of the first alcoholic drinks; barley later served as currency (Sumerian ration tablets).

crops.wild: Wild lentil (Lens culinaris subsp. orientalis / Lens orientalis)
crops.wl: Small bushy herb; wild pods burst open to scatter seeds, and the seeds stay dormant instead of sprouting together.
crops.ch: Pods that stay closed (indehiscent), seeds without dormancy, and seed size rising through the PPNB (Yiftah'el seeds ~4.2 mm wide).
crops.ce: Yiftah'el, Galilee, Israel
crops.cn: Pre-domestication cultivation at Jerf el Ahmar (Syria) and Netiv HaGdud, c. 11,000 cal BP (PPNA); wild lentils gathered at Ohalo II 23,000 BP
crops.dn: Yiftah'el hoard of >1 million lentils, 10,100–9,700 cal BP: widely cultivated; full domestication during the PPNB (one review dates Yiftah'el 6800 BC)
crops.today: 7 Mt dry lentils (2023), 72% from Australia, Canada and India.
crops.fact: At Yiftah'el, Israel, archaeologists found a hoard of more than one million carbonised lentils about 10,000 years old.

crops.wild: Wild pea (Pisum sativum subsp. elatius); P. fulvum gave a second, separate domestication
crops.wl: Climbing wild vine of the Mediterranean and Near East; ripe pods split open to shed seeds, which have rough coats and stay dormant.
crops.ch: Pods that stay shut, seeds that sprout without dormancy, smoother seed coats and bigger seeds; genomics shows two independent domestications.
crops.ce: Southern Turkey / Fertile Crescent (Çayönü area)
crops.cn: A Neolithic founder crop, domesticated in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic (10,500–7,500 years ago); exact start unclear
crops.dn: Smooth-coated domestic peas 5850–5600 BC; Wikipedia: seeds with domestic traits ≥7,000 years old in Turkey (slow change)
sp: Pea finds date back to 4000 BC
crops.today: 21.5 Mt green peas (2023); China and India grow 86%.
crops.fact: Gregor Mendel's mid-19th-century pea crosses founded genetics, but were ignored until about 1900.

crops.wild: Cicer reticulatum (closest wild relative, interfertile)
crops.wl: Rare wild annual of a small area of SE Turkey and nearby Syria; smaller seeds that need a dormancy period and ripen unevenly.
crops.ch: Large palatable seeds without dormancy, seeds easy to free from pods, even ripening, and a shift to spring sowing.
crops.ce: Çayönü, SE Turkey
crops.cn: Chickpeas with other pulses at Tell el-Kerkh and Abu Hureyra, Syria, 8th millennium BCE
crops.dn: Çayönü, 7500–6800 BCE; cultivation of domestic crops documented from 7500 BCE
sp: Spanish and Portuguese bring chickpeas, 16th century
crops.today: India grows 75% of the world's chickpeas (2023).
crops.fact: Genomes of 3,366 chickpeas show a strong bottleneck about 10,000 years ago, the mark of domestication.

crops.wild: Pale flax (Linum bienne)
crops.wl: Slender pale-blue flax from Western Europe to the Caucasus; its wild fibres were spun and dyed 30,000 years ago (Dzudzuana Cave).
crops.ch: First selected for oil: bigger seeds (Tell Ramad); later tall fibre types for linen. Early domesticates still had seed capsules that split open.
crops.ce: Tell Ramad, Syria
crops.cn: First appears at Tell es-Sultan (Jericho), c. 9900–9550 years ago
crops.dn: Domestic oilseed flax with larger seeds at Tell Ramad, and flax fabric at Çatalhöyük, by c. 9,000 years ago
sp: Flax reaches Switzerland and Germany by 5,000 years ago
crops.today: 876,000 t fibre flax (2022), 75% grown in France.
crops.fact: Ancient Egyptian priests wore only linen, and mummies were wrapped in it.

crops.wild: Wild olive / oleaster (Olea europaea var. sylvestris)
crops.wl: Wild olive trees have smaller, thinner-fleshed fruits than cultivated trees.
crops.ch: Bigger, fleshier, oil-rich fruit; good trees cloned by cuttings, layering or grafting, because trees from seed yield poorly.
crops.ce: Galilee (Ein Zippori area)
crops.cn: By 6000 BC olives were turned into oil in Galilee (wild or tended trees unclear)
crops.dn: First cultivated in the eastern Mediterranean 6000–4000 BC; exact date and place unclear (debated)
sp: Submerged settlement south of Haifa (Kfar Samir)
Earliest olive oil amphorae, Early Minoan, 3500 BC
Palace archives record royal olive lands, 2400 BC
Olives reach the Americas, 16th century (sources differ)
crops.today: Spain makes about 25% of world olive oil; the EU nearly 60%.
crops.fact: About 100,000 years ago people on Morocco's Atlantic coast used olive wood for fuel and probably ate olives.

crops.wild: Wild grapevine (Vitis vinifera subsp. sylvestris)
crops.wl: Forest climber with male and female flowers on separate plants; only pollinated females bear small (~6 mm) dark berries.
crops.ch: Hermaphrodite self-pollinating flowers; much bigger berries (up to 3 cm), green, red or black; narrower pips.
crops.ce: Gadachrili Gora, Kvemo Kartli, Georgia
crops.cn: Earliest domesticated grapes and wine residues at Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveri, Georgia, c. 6000 BC
crops.dn: Gadachrili Gora c. 6000 BC; pip-shape studies instead suggest 4100–3000 BC (debated)
sp: Wine residues in jars, c. 5000 BC
Vineyards in Peru by the 1550s, Chile soon after
crops.today: Vitis vinifera grapes make the majority of the world's wine.
crops.fact: Armenia's Areni-1 cave held a 6,000-year-old winery: wine press, fermentation vats, jars and cups.

crops.wild: Uncertain: wild/feral Phoenix dactylifera; North African dates also share genome with Cretan Phoenix theophrasti
crops.wl: Tall palm with separate male and female trees; only females bear fruit, and only when wind carries pollen from a male.
crops.ch: Hand-pollination, so one male can serve up to 100 females; growers keep mostly fruiting females and select sweet varieties.
crops.ce: Eastern Arabia / Persian Gulf (Dalma island, UAE)
crops.cn: Claimed date cultivation at Mehrgarh, Pakistan, c. 7000 BCE; Arabia since the 6th millennium BCE
crops.dn: Archaeological date cultivation in eastern Arabia, 5530–5320 cal BC; origin region debated (Gulf, Mesopotamia–Egypt or India)
sp: Introduced to Mexico as early as the 16th century
Mission San Diego de Alcalá, California
Spaniards bring dates to California by 1769
crops.today: 9.9 Mt dates (2024); Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Algeria and Iran grow 63%.
crops.fact: A 2,000-year-old Judean date seed sprouted into a palm named Methuselah; seven ancient seeds have now grown.

crops.wild: Wild fig / caprifig (wild Ficus carica)
crops.wl: Wild figs depend on the tiny fig wasp Blastophaga psenes; without pollination the fruit tends to drop.
crops.ch: A seedless parthenocarpic mutant that ripens without wasps; kept alive only by planting cut branches (vegetative propagation).
crops.ce: Gilgal I, Jordan Valley (13 km north of Jericho)
crops.cn: Nine parthenocarpic figs, c. 9400–9200 BC, stored with wild barley, wild oats and acorns at Gilgal I
crops.dn: Interpreted as planted, domesticated figs ~1,000 years before cereals (debated: could be wild unpollinated figs, Lev-Yadun et al. 2006)
sp: Greek writers describe tying wild figs to cultivated trees
De Agri Cultura lists five fig strains
Junípero Serra's missionaries bring first figs
True Smyrna figs introduced by Rixford
crops.today: 1.26 Mt figs (2020); Turkey grows a quarter.
crops.fact: Gilgal's figs may be the oldest known crop, about a thousand years before wheat and barley (debated).

crops.wild: Wild Sorghum bicolor (wild races; usually named subsp. verticilliflorum — not stated in Wikipedia)
crops.wl: Tall wild savanna grass of north-east Africa; ripe grains drop from the head (shattering).
crops.ch: Non-shattering heads holding up to 3,000 seeds; first race (bicolor) kept tight husks; later races caudatum, durra and guinea suited new regions.
crops.ce: Kassala, eastern Sudan (Atbara–Gash rivers)
crops.cn: Not separately dated
crops.dn: Domesticated sorghum near Kassala, 3500–3000 BCE (Butana Group); domesticated >5,000 years ago
sp: Sorghum bread in graves, c. 3100 BCE
Reaches West Africa about 3,000 years ago
Spread by the Arab Agricultural Revolution, Middle Ages
crops.today: World's fifth most important cereal; 57 Mt (2023), US grows 14%.
crops.fact: A piece of sorghum bread from a Predynastic Egyptian grave, about 5,100 years old, is in Turin's Egyptian Museum.

crops.wild: Wild pearl millet (Pennisetum violaceum, classed within P. glaucum since 1977)
crops.wl: Bristly wild grass of the southern Sahara and Sahel with small grains that fall when ripe (shattering).
crops.ch: Non-shattering heads, larger grains and stalked spikelet clusters; extremely hardy—grows where drought, poor soil and heat defeat maize or wheat.
crops.ce: Tilemsi Valley, northern Mali
crops.cn: Isozyme studies: domestication north-east of the Senegal River, tentatively c. 6000 BC (estimate)
crops.dn: Domesticated pearl millet impressed in pottery, Tilemsi Valley, Mali, 2500–2000 BCE (Manning et al. 2011)
sp: Western branch of millet farming, after 2000 cal BC
Kintampo farmers (2500–1400 BCE) take millet south
crops.today: Most widely grown millet; India is the largest producer.
crops.fact: In Nigeria it is grown mixed with sorghum and cowpea, so one crop's failure never ruins the whole harvest.

crops.wild: Wild African rice (Oryza barthii)
crops.wl: Wild rice of open West African wetlands; its seed heads shatter, scattering the grains as they ripen.
crops.ch: Less shattering (though on average about half the grains still fall); hardy: tolerates deep water, drought, iron toxicity and poor soils.
crops.ce: Inner Niger Delta, Mali
crops.cn: Not separately dated; wild rice retreated with the drying climate and came to rely on people
crops.dn: Domesticated about 3,000 years ago in the inland delta of the Upper Niger
sp: Carried on slave ships, arriving probably by the 1550s
Asian rice arrives late 1800s and gradually replaces it
crops.today: About 20% of West Africa's commercial rice; mostly replaced by Asian rice.
crops.fact: Enslaved West African rice farmers brought both the seed and the know-how; planters marketed captives for their rice skills.

crops.wild: Wild Coffea arabica of Ethiopian forests (itself a natural hybrid of C. canephora × C. eugenioides)
crops.wl: Forest tree 9–12 m tall with open branches, wild in south Ethiopia, South Sudan's Boma Plateau and Yemen.
crops.ch: Grown as pruned shrubs on terraced Yemeni slopes; nearly all arabica varieties descend from plants farmed in Yemen.
crops.ce: Haraz Mountains, Yemen (wild origin: SW Ethiopia)
crops.cn: Cultivated in Yemen's highlands (Haraz, Bani Matar) by the 15th century; no confirmed coffee drinking earlier
crops.dn: Same: Yemen became the first large-scale production zone; Harar tradition in Ethiopia
sp: Gabriel de Clieu brings seedlings to the New World
Becomes world's largest coffee producer by 1852
crops.today: Arabica is about 60% of world coffee production.
crops.fact: Arabica was born as a natural hybrid of two coffee species between 1.08 million and 543,000 years ago.

crops.wild: Wild and semi-wild groves of the same species, West and south-west Africa (Angola to the Gambia)
crops.wl: Tall African palm bearing large bunches of oily fruit, each around a thick-shelled nut.
crops.ch: Modern tenera palms (thick-shelled dura × shell-less pisifera) have thin shells: about 30% more oil per fruit.
crops.ce: Kintampo, Ghana (early use); domesticated along West Africa's Atlantic coast
crops.cn: Oil palm used at Kintampo starting at least 4,000 years ago
crops.dn: Semi-domesticated in West Africa; no clear date
sp: Possible palm oil in tomb (doubtful: maybe date oil)
Dutch introduce oil palms to Java
Introduced to British Malaya by Sime and Darby
crops.today: Palm oil ~36% of oil-crop oils (2017); Indonesia produced 60% (2022).
crops.fact: The palm-nut vulture lives largely on oil palm fruit: over 60% of an adult's diet, over 90% of a juvenile's.

crops.wild: Common wild rice (Oryza rufipogon)
crops.wl: Marsh grass whose awned grains drop (shatter) as they ripen, so most seed fell before anyone could harvest it.
crops.ch: Non-shattering spikelets, shorter or no awns, upright dense plants. At Tianluoshan non-shattering spikelet bases rose from 27% to 39% in c. 300 years.
crops.ce: Lower Yangtze, Zhejiang (Shangshan; Tianluoshan near Hemudu)
crops.cn: Shangshan rice phytoliths directly dated c. 9,400 cal BP, already closer to domestic forms (Zuo et al. 2017); Wikipedia gives domestication 13,500-8,200 years ago
crops.dn: Tianluoshan: non-shattering spikelet bases 27%->39% between 6,900 and 6,600 years ago (Fuller et al. 2009); domestication was gradual (debated pace)
sp: Rice reaches Sino-Tibetan north by 6,000-5,600 years ago
Japonica arrives c. 4,500 years ago; crosses into indica
crops.today: Staple food of over half the world's people; 800 million t harvested in 2023.
crops.fact: Indica rice arose when japonica reached India c. 4,500 years ago and crossed with local wild or proto-indica rice.

crops.wild: Green foxtail (Setaria viridis)
crops.wl: Weedy grass with small bristly heads of tiny grains that shatter (fall off) as soon as they ripen.
crops.ch: Grains stay on the head (non-shattering, the main wild/crop difference per Zohary & Hopf); bigger, heavier drooping heads with larger grains.
crops.ce: Cishan, Hebei (Taihang foothills)
crops.cn: Foxtail millet joins broomcorn millet in Cishan storage pits after c. 8,700 cal BP (Lu et al. 2009); early Cishan dates questioned by some (debated)
crops.dn: Cishan culture identified as earliest to domesticate foxtail millet, c. 6500-5500 BC (Wikipedia)
sp: First foxtail millet outside its native range
Earliest directly dated in Southeast Asia
First definite Near East evidence, Iron Age
crops.today: Second most widely planted millet and the most grown millet in Asia.
crops.fact: Though domesticated by 6000 BC in China, foxtail millet only reached central Europe in the 2nd millennium BC.

crops.wild: Uncertain: weedy Panicum miliaceum subsp. ruderale may be the wild ancestor or a feral escape (debated)
crops.wl: Wild ancestor not securely known; weedy forms drop their small round seeds when ripe.
crops.ch: Seeds retained on the plant and larger grain; a very short life cycle - early varieties ripened as little as 45 days after planting.
crops.ce: Cishan, Hebei (Taihang foothills)
crops.cn: Husk phytoliths and biomolecules of common millet in Cishan storage pits, c. 10,300-8,700 cal BP (Lu et al. 2009); early dates questioned (debated)
crops.dn: Earliest archaeological evidence for domesticated proso at Cishan, c. 8000 BCE (Wikipedia)
sp: Directly dated grains; older Neolithic claims overturned
crops.today: Needs little water; some varieties give grain only 60 days after planting.
crops.fact: Common millet was East Asia's earliest dry-farming crop, probably thanks to its excellent drought resistance (Lu et al. 2009).

crops.wild: Wild soybean (Glycine soja)
crops.wl: Annual wild legume of China, Japan, Korea and the Russian Far East with small seeds, much smaller than today's soybeans.
crops.ch: Selection for big seeds: small-seeded soy at 9,000-8,600 cal BP in north China; large seeds in Japan by 5,000 and Korea by 3,000 cal BP.
crops.ce: Between the Yellow and Huai rivers (Jiahu, Henan)
crops.cn: Charred wild soybean at Jiahu (9,000-7,800 years ago); Wikipedia cites domestication evidence 7000-6600 BC in China; genetics: 6,000-9,000 years ago
crops.dn: Seeds significantly larger than wild in Middle Jomon Japan (5,000 cal BP, direct AMS dates; Lee et al. 2011). Single vs multiple domestication is debated
sp: Grown as a food crop c. 1000-900 BC
First New World crop, seeds from Samuel Bowen
Low-latitude cultivars make Brazil a top producer
crops.today: Over 353 million t in 2020; Brazil and the USA grow two thirds.
crops.fact: The word 'soy' comes from Japanese shoyu (soy sauce) via the Kagoshima dialect form 'soi' - the bean is named after its sauce.

crops.wild: Unknown: no wild populations of China-type tea are known, so its origin is speculative
crops.wl: Evergreen shrub or tree up to 20 m tall; wild leaves larger than cultivated ones, bitter and astringent with caffeine.
crops.ch: Kept as bushes pruned to about 1 m for plucking young leaves; genetics suggest Chinese and Indian Assam tea were domesticated separately.
crops.ce: Yunnan, borderlands of SW China, NE India and Myanmar
crops.cn: Tea drinking likely began in Yunnan in the 2nd millennium BC as a medicine (Wikipedia; estimate)
crops.dn: Oldest physical tea: leaves in the mausoleum of Emperor Jing of Han (d. 141 BC), Xi'an, found 2016; first written record 59 BC; first record of cultivation on Meng Mountain near Chengdu
sp: Dutch East India Company brings first tea, early 17th c.
Tea gifted by China to Tsar Michael I
Pepys drinks his first 'cup of tee'
British introduce tea cultivation to India
crops.today: After plain water, the most widely consumed drink in the world.
crops.fact: Chinese small-leaf tea and Assam tea are estimated to have split c. 22,000 years ago - long before anyone brewed it.

crops.wild: Robust cane (Saccharum robustum), New Guinea
crops.wl: Tall wild cane of New Guinea; its fibrous stems held far less sweet juice than the cultivated canes bred from it (general literature).
crops.ch: Selected for thick, juicy, sweet stems, propagated from stem cuttings; hybrids with wild S. spontaneum gave the hardy canes of Asia.
crops.ce: New Guinea highlands (Kuk Swamp)
crops.cn: Kuk Swamp: evidence of banana and sugarcane cultivation 6,900-6,400 years ago
crops.dn: Several strains selectively bred from S. robustum from c. 6,000 BP (Wikipedia)
sp: Austronesian traders bring cane by c. 3,000 BP
Arab traders spread sugar from India, c. 8th c.
crops.today: World's largest crop by weight: 1.9 billion t in 2020, 40% from Brazil.
crops.fact: Papuans and Austronesians first grew sugarcane mainly as food for their domesticated pigs. Crystalline sugar was first made in northern India.

crops.wild: Wild banana Musa acuminata (esp. subsp. banksii) and Musa balbisiana
crops.wl: Wild bananas are packed with numerous large, hard seeds and little pulp.
crops.ch: Seedless (parthenocarpic) fruit, first picked from natural seedless plants; hybrid triploids propagated as clones from suckers - e.g. Cavendish.
crops.ce: Kuk Swamp, New Guinea highlands
crops.cn: Banana phytoliths at Kuk Swamp c. 10,000-6,500 BP; plant exploitation on the wetland margin 10,220-9,910 cal BP
crops.dn: Bananas intensively cultivated by at least 6,950-6,440 cal BP, Kuk Swamp (Denham et al. 2003)
sp: Austronesian settlers bring bananas, c. 600 AD
Portuguese bring bananas from West Africa, 16th c.
crops.today: India and China grew about 26% of the world's bananas in 2022.
crops.fact: The banana plant is the largest herbaceous flowering plant: no wood, yet most are about 5 m tall.

crops.wild: Wild taro (wild forms of Colocasia esculenta)
crops.wl: Raw corms and leaves are acrid and toxic: needle-shaped calcium oxalate crystals (raphides) irritate mouth and throat.
crops.ch: Larger, less acrid corms grown from offsets; preferred over other Pacific 'taros' as less likely to contain irritating raphides.
crops.ce: Kuk Swamp, New Guinea highlands
crops.cn: Taro used at Kuk Swamp 8250-7960 BC; wild vs cultivated cannot be told apart
crops.dn: No clear date: likely domesticated several times (New Guinea, mainland SE Asia, NE India); wild and cultivated taro are hard to tell apart
sp: Taro starch at Lapita sites 1100-550 BC
Polynesian settlers arrive 940-1200 AD; taro becomes poi
crops.today: 18 million t produced in 2022; Nigeria grew 46% of it.
crops.fact: Starch on stone tools shows taro was used at Kilu Cave, Solomon Islands, some 28,000-20,000 years ago.

crops.wild: Not a wild species: hybrid of pomelo (Citrus maxima) and mandarin (Citrus reticulata)
crops.wl: No wild sweet orange exists. Its ancestors, wild pomelo and mandarin, descend from small berries; some mandarins are too sour to eat.
crops.ch: One ancient cross, about 42% pomelo and 58% mandarin; every sweet orange is a clone of it, differing only by selected bud mutations (e.g. navel).
crops.ce: Southern China, NE India and Myanmar (Citrus genus: SE Himalayan foothills)
crops.cn: Earliest mention of the sweet orange in Chinese literature, 314 BC; the date of the original cross is unknown
crops.dn: Arose in domestication in East Asia; no archaeological date
sp: Columbus may have planted oranges on 2nd voyage
Italian and Portuguese merchants bring sweet orange, c. 1500
crops.today: 67 million t of oranges grown in 2024; Brazil produced 23%.
crops.fact: Grapefruit is a sweet orange x pomelo backcross; clementines come from orange x mandarin crosses.

crops.wild: Exact wild ancestor unknown (Old World A-genome cottons)
crops.wl: Shrub 1-2 m tall with maple-like leaves; seeds sit in capsules (bolls) covered in fibre hairs.
crops.ch: Selected for long, plentiful spinnable fibre (lint) on the seeds (general literature).
crops.ce: Mehrgarh, Balochistan, Pakistan
crops.cn: Mineralised cotton thread in a string of copper beads at Mehrgarh, 6th millennium BC (Mehrgarh period I dating debated: 7000 vs 5250-4650 BCE). Dyed cotton fibres at Tel Tsaf, Jordan Valley, 5200 BCE, possibly traded from South Asia
crops.dn: Cotton textiles and spindle whorls at Mohenjo-daro, 3rd millennium BCE; Indus Valley likely site of first cultivation of G. arboreum
sp: Cotton spinning flourishes (G. herbaceum); 85% of textiles
Grown in Yunnan under the Han dynasty
Muslim conquests bring cotton making to Europe
Cotton weaving spreads after Norman conquest of Sicily
crops.today: Upland cotton from Mexico gives 90% of world output; India is the largest producer.
crops.fact: Megasthenes told Seleucus I of Indian 'trees on which wool grows' - probably tree cotton.

crops.wild: Balsas teosinte (Zea mays subsp. parviglumis)
crops.wl: Short, bushy grass; each tiny 'ear' holds 5-10 seeds, each sealed in a very hard fruitcase, and the ear breaks apart when ripe.
crops.ch: One tall stalk (gene tb1), naked kernels held on a cob that does not shatter: 8-32 rows, up to 1,200 grains on a large ear.
crops.ce: Central Balsas River valley, Guerrero (Xihuatoxtla shelter)
crops.cn: Genetics: single domestication about 9,000 years ago from Balsas teosinte (Doebley and colleagues)
crops.dn: Maize starch grains and phytoliths at Xihuatoxtla shelter, 8,700 cal BP (Piperno et al. 2009); oldest cobs from Guila Naquitz, Oaxaca
sp: Maize reaches the Andes at least 8,000 years ago
First maize in the US Southwest, c. 4,100 years ago
Arrives after 200 BCE; later replaces local crops
Grown in Spain around 1525, decades after Columbus
crops.today: 1.16 billion t in 2020: the top grain crop, second only to sugarcane overall.
crops.fact: Maize and teosinte look so different that the teosinte origin was only proposed in 1931-32 (Vavilov, Beadle); two genes explain much of it.

crops.wild: Wild C. pepo: subsp. fraterna (NE Mexico) and subsp. texana / var. ozarkana (eastern USA)
crops.wl: Small hard-rinded gourds with bitter, toxic cucurbitacin in the flesh; eaten mainly for seeds or used as containers.
crops.ch: Loss of bitterness, bigger fruits with thicker rind and fewer, larger seeds; Guila Naquitz peduncles over 10 mm thick by 8,000 BP.
crops.ce: Guila Naquitz Cave, Oaxaca
crops.cn: Cucurbita seeds and rinds at Guila Naquitz from c. 8750 BC (4% of rinds); oldest known locations Oaxaca 10,000-8,000 years ago
crops.dn: Thicker rinds and peduncles show deliberate breeding by no later than 8,000 BP at Guila Naquitz
sp: Separate eastern domestication; present 4,000 years ago
Domesticated squash in the Eastern Agricultural Complex
crops.today: One species gives pumpkins, zucchini, pattypans and ornamental gourds; record pumpkin 1,246.9 kg (2023).
crops.fact: Wild squashes were probably spread by mammoths and mastodons; after these megafauna died out, people became their seed dispersers (Kistler et al. 2015).

crops.wild: Wild common bean (wild Phaseolus vulgaris), Mexico to Argentina
crops.wl: A climbing vine with small beans; raw beans contain toxic phytohaemagglutinin, destroyed only by long boiling.
crops.ch: Larger seeds, bush (non-climbing) forms, and many seed colours; domesticated twice, giving separate Mesoamerican and Andean gene pools.
crops.ce: Mesoamerica and the southern Andes (two centres)
crops.cn: Genetics and archaeology: domesticated separately in Mesoamerica and the southern Andes some 8,000 years ago (Wikipedia)
crops.dn: Large-seeded domesticated beans in the highlands of Peru, 2300 BC; small-seeded beans in Mexico by 300 BC
sp: Large-seeded Andean beans reach the coast
Small-seeded Mexican beans spread north by 1000 AD
Arrives in the 16th century via the Columbian Exchange
crops.today: 28 million t of dry beans in 2022; India grew 23%.
crops.fact: The 'beans' Romans and Greeks ate were Old World species; P. vulgaris joined maize and squash as the 'Three Sisters'.

crops.wild: Wild potatoes of the Solanum brevicaule complex (northern group, Peru)
crops.wl: About twenty similar wild tuber-bearing species; wild tubers are small, and potato plants contain toxic glycoalkaloids such as solanine.
crops.ch: Bigger tubers with negligible glycoalkaloids; tubers that no longer need short autumn days to form; over 5,000 varieties today.
crops.ce: Southern Peru / NW Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca
crops.cn: Domesticated in southern Peru and extreme NW Bolivia between 8000 and 5000 BC (single origin from the northern S. brevicaule complex: Spooner et al. 2005)
crops.dn: Earliest verified potato tubers at Ancon, central Peru, 2500 BC; stone-tool residues suggest 3400 BC
sp: Receipt for potatoes shipped Las Palmas-Antwerp
First wide-scale European crop, early 17th c.
Mentioned at a banquet in Ajmer
crops.today: China and India lead world potato production (2023).
crops.fact: Over 99% of today's potato varieties descend from a subspecies of the lowlands of south-central Chile, not the Andes.

crops.wild: Currant tomato (Solanum pimpinellifolium), Ecuador and Peru
crops.wl: Wild 'currant tomato' with tiny red fruits - small enough to be named after currants.
crops.ch: Much larger fruits - via the cherry tomato (var. cerasiforme) - and lumpy, many-chambered Mesoamerican forms; many colours.
crops.ce: Western South America (Ecuador-Peru); possibly Mesoamerica (debated)
crops.cn: Genomic estimate: cultivated tomato originated c. 7,000 years ago, with substantial uncertainty (debated)
crops.dn: Already cultivated in southern Mexico by 500 BCE; exact date and place of domestication unknown
sp: Aztec markets sell many tomato varieties
Introduced via the Philippines or Macau, 16th c.
Long thought poisonous; common in markets by 1820
crops.today: 192 million t in 2023; China grew 36%.
crops.fact: In 1548 Cosimo de' Medici's steward reported a basket of tomatoes 'arrived safely' - yet Tuscans long used them only as table decoration.

crops.wild: Chiltepin / bird pepper (Capsicum annuum var. glabriusculum)
crops.wl: Bushy shrub with tiny, fiercely hot berries (chiltepin: 100,000-200,000 Scoville units) eaten and spread by birds.
crops.ch: Much larger fruits of many shapes and colours; heat bred from fiery to none (bell pepper: 0 Scoville).
crops.ce: Central-east Mexico (Tehuacan Valley, Puebla)
crops.cn: Wild chilies eaten more than 8,000 years ago (Oaxaca, Tehuacan caves); Capsicum in human diets since c. 7500 BC
crops.dn: Domestication about 6,000 years ago in Mexico; central-east Mexico supported by four lines of evidence (Kraft et al. 2014)
sp: Chanca brings chilies from Columbus's 2nd voyage
Portuguese carry chilies to Africa and Asia, 16th c.
Reaches East Asia in the late 16th century
crops.today: 45 million t of fresh chillies and peppers in 2024; China grew 39%.
crops.fact: Capsaicin deters mammals but birds feel nothing - so the wild seeds are spread by birds.

crops.wild: Wild cacao (Theobroma cacao) of the upper Amazon
crops.wl: Understorey tree with flowers and pods directly on the trunk; 20-60 bitter seeds in sweet white pulp.
crops.ch: First grown probably for the sweet pulp (snack, mild alcoholic drink); later for fermented, roasted beans - Criollo, Forastero, Nacional types.
crops.ce: Santa Ana-La Florida, Zamora-Chinchipe, Ecuador
crops.cn: Cacao starch, theobromine residues and ancient DNA at Santa Ana-La Florida, c. 5,300 years ago (Zarrillo et al. 2018)
crops.dn: Upper Amazon (Mayo-Chinchipe culture) is the oldest known centre of cacao domestication; Mesoamerican origin no longer favoured
sp: Paso de la Amada area, Chiapas
Mokaya drink frothy cacao by 1900 BC
Q'eqchi' Maya nobles bring chocolate to the court
Tetteh Quarshie plants cacao from Fernando Po
crops.today: 5.6 million t of cocoa beans in 2023; Ivory Coast grew 42.5%.
crops.fact: Cacao flowers are pollinated by tiny biting midges (Forcipomyia), not bees. In 1545 thirty beans bought a small rabbit.

crops.wild: Manihot esculenta subsp. flabellifolia
crops.wl: Woody shrub of the southern Amazon fringe without the crop's big swollen storage roots (general literature).
crops.ch: Big starchy storage roots, grown from stem cuttings; sweet and bitter varieties - bitter ones need careful processing to remove cyanide.
crops.ce: Southern border of the Amazon basin, west-central Brazil
crops.cn: Likely first domesticated in west-central Brazil no more than 10,000 years ago (Olsen & Schaal 1999 genetics; estimate)
crops.dn: Manioc pollen in the Gulf of Mexico lowlands (San Andres, Tabasco), c. 4600 BC; oldest direct cultivation evidence Joya de Ceren, El Salvador, c. 600 AD
sp: Single manioc pollen grain, far from its homeland
Maya fields buried by volcanic ash
Portuguese bring cassava from Brazil, 16th c.
Spread to Asian colonies by Portuguese and Spanish
crops.today: Third-largest carbohydrate source in the tropics; over 500 million people depend on it.
crops.fact: Improperly prepared cassava can contain enough cyanide to poison; yet farmers may choose bitter varieties to minimise crop losses.

crops.wild: Wild common sunflower (Helianthus annuus), central and western North America
crops.wl: Branched plant carrying many small flower heads instead of one big one.
crops.ch: A single huge flower head on one unbranched stem, with large seeds (achenes) for snacks and oil.
crops.ce: Eastern North America (Riverton site, Illinois); Mexico also proposed (debated)
crops.cn: Long held: domesticated in the southeastern US roughly 5,000 years ago
crops.dn: Earliest fully domesticated US sunflower, Tennessee, c. 2300 BCE; a domesticated seed from San Andres, Tabasco, c. 2650-2550 BCE suggests Mexico (debated)
sp: Grown with goosefoot and squash, Eastern Agricultural Complex
Spanish explorers carry seeds to Europe
crops.today: Russia and Ukraine produce over half the world's sunflower seed (2020).
crops.fact: Russian Orthodox Lent allowed only plant fats, so sunflower oil boomed in 18th-century Russia.

crops.wild: Grey wolf (Canis lupus), a Late Pleistocene wolf population that is now extinct
crops.wl: Pack-living hunters of the Ice Age steppe-tundra, larger and stronger-jawed than most dogs; they followed the same big game as human hunters.
crops.ch: Smaller teeth and skull, shorter snout, tameness and a long puppy-like phase; later starch digestion (more AMY2B copies) and hundreds of shapes and coats.
crops.ce: Northern Eurasia, exact place unknown; Siberia proposed (Perri et al. 2021), Europe and East Asia also argued (debated)
crops.cn: Genetic estimates: dog lineage split from wolves 20,000–40,000 years ago; Perri et al. 2021 place domestication in Siberia c. 23,000 years ago. Older 'Palaeolithic dogs' (Goyet, Razboinichya, up to 36,000 years) are disputed. Debated.
crops.dn: Bonn–Oberkassel dog, buried with two humans c. 14,200 years ago, is the earliest widely accepted dog (Erralla, Spain, c. 17,500 years has also been proposed).
sp: Natufian burial of a woman with a puppy, c. 12,000 years ago
Oldest dated dog remains in North America, c. 10,150 years ago; dogs probably came with the first Americans (debated)
Sled dogs bred for hauling c. 9,500 years ago
Oldest dingo remains, c. 3,300–3,100 years ago; dingoes came by sea from Southeast Asia
Greenland sled dogs arrive with the Inuit c. 850 years ago and stay isolated since
crops.today: Some 700 million to 1 billion dogs live worldwide, most of them free-ranging village and street dogs.
crops.fact: The dog was domesticated by Ice Age hunter-gatherers, thousands of years before anyone farmed a plant or herded a sheep.

crops.wild: Asiatic mouflon (Ovis gmelini, syn. O. orientalis)
crops.wl: Short-haired, reddish-brown wild sheep of the rocky hills of Anatolia and Iran; rams carry heavy curled horns, and the coat is hair with only a short woolly undercoat that moults.
crops.ch: Smaller body and horns (many ewes hornless), floppy ears and long tails, white and spotted coats, and a fleece of continuously growing wool that must be shorn.
crops.ce: Upper Euphrates–Tigris and Zagros foothills (SE Turkey, N Iraq, W Iran)
crops.cn: Kill-off patterns (young males culled) in SE Anatolia and the Zagros c. 9000–8500 BCE; Wikipedia gives 11,000–9000 BC for domestication in Mesopotamia.
crops.dn: Larson et al. 2014: domestic sheep c. 10,500 years ago (c. 8500 BCE).
sp: Sheep, goats, dogs and probably cattle and pigs shipped to Cyprus by the first farmers, c. 8800–8600 BCE
Sheep reach the Indus borderlands c. 7000 BCE (Mehrgarh dating debated; newer dates c. 5250 BCE)
Farmers bring sheep and goats into Europe
Figurines suggest selection for woolly sheep; woven wool garments by c. 4000 BCE
Sheep reach northern China c. 5,000–4,500 years ago, probably via the Hexi Corridor
Sheep arrive with the First Fleet; Australia later becomes the world's wool giant
crops.today: About 540 million sheep are slaughtered for meat each year; the living flock is about 1.2 billion (2019).
crops.fact: Early sheep were kept for meat, milk and hides; the woolly fleece only appeared thousands of years after domestication.

crops.wild: Bezoar ibex (Capra aegagrus), the wild goat
crops.wl: Agile wild goat of the cliffs of the Zagros, Taurus and Caucasus; bucks have long scimitar-shaped horns and a dark beard and shoulder stripe.
crops.ch: Smaller, with twisted or shorter horns, floppy ears and all colours; bred for milk, meat, hair (cashmere, mohair) and hardiness.
crops.ce: Zagros Mountains, western Iran (Ganj Dareh); probably several sources in the Fertile Crescent
crops.cn: Zeder & Hesse 2000: managed goat herds (young-male cull) at Ganj Dareh c. 10,000 years ago.
crops.dn: Size reduction and domestic goats at Jericho, Çayönü and others c. 8,000–9,000 years ago; aDNA shows several wild source populations (Daly et al. 2018).
sp: Goats, sheep and cattle herded at Mehrgarh (dating debated: c. 7000 or c. 5250 BCE)
Goats enter Europe with the first farmers
Goats and sheep from the Levant reach Egypt c. 6000 BCE, probably via Sinai
Herders bring goats, sheep and cattle into East Africa
Spanish conquistadors bring goats to the Americas in the 16th century
crops.today: About 1.18 billion goats lived worldwide in 2024, most in India, China and Nigeria.
crops.fact: At Ganj Dareh the herd profile shows that people culled young males 10,000 years ago, while the bones still looked fully wild.

crops.wild: Wild boar (Sus scrofa)
crops.wl: Bristly dark forest pig with a long snout, tusks and striped piglets; lives in family groups and roots for food in woods and marshes.
crops.ch: Shorter snout and legs, curly tails, floppy ears, pink or spotted skin, fast growth and big litters; behaviour calmer around people.
crops.ce: Upper Tigris, SE Turkey (Çayönü); a second, independent centre in China
crops.cn: Wild boar shipped to Cyprus more than 11,400 years ago, implying management on the mainland (Vigne et al.).
crops.dn: Larson et al. 2014: domestic pigs c. 10,500 years ago in SW Asia (Çayönü); China c. 8,000 years ago.
sp: Pigs domesticated independently from East Asian wild boar c. 8,000 years ago (second centre)
Near Eastern pigs reach Europe at least 8,500 years ago, then mix with local wild boar
Austronesian seafarers carry pigs, chickens and dogs into the Pacific
Columbus's second voyage lands pigs in the Americas
crops.today: About 1 billion domestic pigs live today; China produces nearly half of the world’s pork.
crops.fact: European pigs kept their domestic looks but today carry less than 5% Near Eastern DNA, because they interbred with local wild boar for 3,000 years.

crops.wild: Aurochs (Bos primigenius), extinct since 1627
crops.wl: Huge wild ox, bulls up to 1.8 m at the shoulder, black with a pale back stripe and long forward-curving horns; lived in open woods and river valleys across Eurasia and North Africa.
crops.ch: Much smaller and calmer, many coat colours, smaller horns (or none); later bred for milk, meat and pulling ploughs and carts.
crops.ce: Upper Euphrates and Tigris valleys (N Syria, SE Turkey; Dja'de, Çayönü)
crops.cn: Size change and management of aurochs at Dja'de el-Mughara and Çayönü c. 8800–8300 BCE (Helmer et al.).
crops.dn: Wikipedia: taurine cattle domesticated c. 10,500 years ago in Anatolia, the Levant and W Iran; Bollongino et al. 2012: c. 80 founding cows.
sp: Early farmers ship cattle to Cyprus by boat (Shillourokambos); they die out there in the 8th millennium BCE
Cattle enter Europe with the first farmers
Linear Pottery farmers keep cattle across central Europe
Cattle herders in a green Sahara; claims of a separate African domestication c. 8000 BCE (Nabta Playa) are debated
Columbus's second voyage brings cattle to the Americas
crops.today: Over 940 million cattle were counted in 2022 (taurine and zebu together).
crops.fact: All taurine cattle may descend from only about 80 wild aurochs cows captured in the Near East.

crops.wild: Indian aurochs (Bos primigenius namadicus), extinct
crops.wl: South Asian form of the aurochs, a huge wild ox of the Indian plains; its last remains date to about 3,800 years ago.
crops.ch: Shoulder hump, big dewlap and drooping ears, loose skin; tolerant of heat, drought and ticks.
crops.ce: Mehrgarh, Baluchistan (Pakistan)
crops.cn: Cattle bones at Mehrgarh from the 7th millennium BCE; size decrease of local cattle (Meadow).
crops.dn: Larson et al. 2014: zebu c. 8,000 years ago; Wikipedia Zebu gives 6,000–7,000 years ago at Mehrgarh (estimates differ).
sp: Zebu bulls spread west and mix with taurine cattle during the 4.2-ka drought (Verdugo et al. 2019)
Zebu reaches the Horn c. 1000 CE and the rest of sub-Saharan Africa after 700 CE (Zebu article); arrival in East Africa 3,500–2,500 years ago is also proposed (debated)
Indian zebu breeds imported; Nelore type now dominates Brazilian beef
crops.today: Zebu and zebu-cross cattle make up most of the herds of India, Africa and tropical South America; India alone had 65.7 million draft cattle in 1998.
crops.fact: More than 80% of Brazil’s beef cattle are Nelore or Nelore crosses, descended from Ongole cattle of southern India.

crops.wild: Wild water buffalo (Bubalus arnee)
crops.wl: Massive grey-black wild ox of swamps and river floodplains of India and Southeast Asia, with very wide sweeping horns; spends hot hours wallowing in mud.
crops.ch: Calmer and smaller-horned; two types: river buffalo (India, bred for milk) and swamp buffalo (SE Asia, ploughing paddies), domesticated separately.
crops.ce: River buffalo: western India; swamp buffalo: mainland Southeast Asia (separate domestication)
crops.cn: Phylogenetic estimate: river buffalo domesticated in western India c. 6,300 years ago (c. 4300 BCE); genetic, not archaeological.
crops.dn: Water buffalo on Indus (Harappan) seals c. 2500 BCE; swamp buffalo separately in SE Asia.
sp: Water buffalo shown on Akkadian cylinder seals, brought from the Indus
Swamp buffalo in mainland Southeast Asia, domesticated separately 3,000–7,000 years ago
Butchered domestic buffalo at Nagsabaran, at least 2,500 years ago
River buffalo reach southern Italy in the early Middle Ages (perhaps via Arab Sicily; origin debated); buffalo-milk cheeses recorded from the 12th century
crops.today: About 208 million water buffalo live in 77 countries and give 72 million tonnes of milk a year.
crops.fact: River and swamp buffalo have different numbers of chromosomes (50 and 48); they do not readily interbreed, yet their hybrids can be fertile.

crops.wild: African wildcat (Felis lybica), Near Eastern and North African form
crops.wl: Sandy-grey, faintly striped wildcat with long legs and a ringed tail; a solitary hunter of rodents in dry scrub and around villages.
crops.ch: Hardly changed in body: tamer, smaller brain, more coat colours and patterns (tabby blotches, white, ginger); they largely domesticated themselves by hunting mice in grain stores.
crops.ce: Near East / Fertile Crescent, later Egypt
crops.cn: Shillourokambos, Cyprus, c. 7500–7200 BCE: wildcat buried near a human grave (taming, not necessarily domestication). Debated.
crops.dn: Cats in Egyptian Middle Kingdom art c. 1950 BCE; Ottoni et al. 2017 aDNA: Near Eastern and Egyptian lineages. When cats became fully domestic is debated.
sp: A tomb painting of Baqet III (11th Dynasty) shows a cat facing a rodent; Egypt’s cats later spread around the Mediterranean
Earliest domestic cat in Greece c. 1200 BCE
Domestic cats spread through Europe with Roman trade, c. 2,000 years ago
Egyptian cat lineage reaches a Baltic port by the end of the Western Roman Empire
Domestic cats reach China along the Silk Roads (earlier Chinese 'cats' were tamed leopard cats)
crops.today: An estimated 600 million domestic cats live worldwide, 400 million of them in Asia.
crops.fact: A cat buried beside a person at Shillourokambos, Cyprus, c. 7500 BCE must have been brought by boat, because Cyprus had no wildcats.

crops.wild: Red junglefowl (Gallus gallus), mainly the subspecies G. g. spadiceus
crops.wl: Shy, slender forest-edge bird of Southeast Asia; cocks have red combs, golden hackles and green-black tails, hens are brown; flies well.
crops.ch: Larger and heavier, lays eggs all year (a junglefowl hen lays only a few clutches), many plumage colours, many no longer fly.
crops.ce: Mainland Southeast Asia (central Thailand; Ban Non Wat)
crops.cn: Peters et al. 2022 (PNAS): earliest probable chicken bones at Ban Non Wat, central Thailand, c. 1650–1250 BCE, tied to rice and millet farming.
crops.dn: Same evidence; genomic estimates (up to 8,000 years ago) and older claims from China are debated.
sp: Chickens reach the Mediterranean c. 800 BCE, first as exotic birds
Lapita seafarers carry chickens into Remote Oceania
European ships bring chickens; pre-Columbian chickens in Chile are debated
crops.today: About 74 billion chickens are slaughtered for meat every year, by far the most numerous farm animal.
crops.fact: For centuries after reaching Europe, chickens were kept for cockfighting and as sacred birds, not for eggs or meat.

crops.wild: Wild horse (Equus ferus) of the western Eurasian steppe; the European tarpan survived to the 19th century
crops.wl: Stocky dun wild horse with a big head and upright mane, living in herds on the steppe and hunted by Ice Age people.
crops.ch: Calmer temperament and a stronger back for riding (genes GSDMC and ZFPM1 selected, Librado 2021); later all sizes, coat colours and gaits.
crops.ce: Lower Volga–Don, Pontic–Caspian steppe (aDNA: DOM2 lineage)
crops.cn: Botai culture, Kazakhstan, 3700–3500 BCE: possible bit wear and horse milk; aDNA (Gaunitz 2018) shows these horses fed into Przewalski's horses; management vs. domestication is debated.
crops.dn: Librado et al. 2021 (Nature): DOM2 horses arose in the Volga–Don region c. 2200 BCE and spread rapidly with chariots.
sp: Spoke-wheeled chariots and horse burials c. 2000 BCE
DOM2 horses spread across Eurasia within a few centuries, replacing other horses
Horses and chariots arrive in the Hyksos period
Columbus's second voyage brings horses back to the Americas, where native horses had died out c. 10,000 years earlier
Horses arrive with the First Fleet
crops.today: An estimated 100 million horses, donkeys and mules still work in agriculture and transport.
crops.fact: The famous Botai horses of Kazakhstan turned out to be ancestors of Przewalski's horses, not of today's domestic horses.

crops.wild: African wild ass (Equus africanus), Nubian and probably other now-lost populations
crops.wl: Grey desert ass with long ears, a dark shoulder cross and zebra-striped legs (Somali form); survives on little water in rocky deserts of NE Africa.
crops.ch: Calm, sure-footed pack and riding animal; varied size and colour; wild ass now critically endangered.
crops.ce: East Africa / Horn of Africa (genomics, Todd et al. 2022)
crops.cn: Todd et al. 2022 (Science): genomes point to a single domestication in East Africa c. 5000 BCE (estimate).
crops.dn: Abydos donkey burials c. 3000 BCE (Rossel et al. 2008); Wikipedia: domesticated 5,000–7,000 years ago.
sp: Ten donkeys buried beside an early pharaoh's tomb, with backs worn by loads
Donkeys carry loads across the Near East; kunga hybrids (donkey × Syrian wild ass) pull Sumerian war wagons, c. 2600–2000 BCE
First donkeys in the Americas, from Columbus's second voyage
Pack donkeys imported; up to 5 million feral donkeys today
crops.today: Almost 54 million donkeys lived worldwide in 2024, most in Ethiopia and other African countries.
crops.fact: The donkey is the only major livestock animal domesticated in Africa from a wild animal of Africa (cattle there came from the Near East).

crops.wild: Wild dromedary, extinct (hunted in Arabia until c. 1000 BCE)
crops.wl: One-humped wild camel of the Arabian coasts and deserts, known only from bones and rock art; hunted for meat by Neolithic Arabians.
crops.ch: Tame load-carrier and milk animal able to cross deserts for weeks; still interbreeds little with other camels.
crops.ce: South-east Arabian Peninsula
crops.cn: Wikipedia: first domesticated in southern Arabia c. 4000–3000 BC (early, wild-or-tame camel bones are hard to tell apart).
crops.dn: Almathen et al. 2016: domestic camels in SE Arabia by c. 3,000 years ago; clear domestic remains from the end of the 2nd millennium BCE (estimate).
sp: Earliest domestic camels in the southern Levant, at copper mines c. 930 BCE
Dromedaries are in use south of the Sahara, in the Senegal valley, by the 3rd century CE; later they carry trans-Saharan trade
Dromedaries imported for desert exploration; today the world's largest feral herd
crops.today: FAO counted about 10 million dromedaries in eastern Africa alone already in 1984; Somalia and Sudan hold the biggest herds.
crops.fact: The only wild dromedaries left are feral, mainly in Australia, descended from 19th-century imports.

crops.wild: An extinct wild two-humped camel of Central Asia (the living wild Bactrian camel, C. ferus, is a separate species, not the ancestor)
crops.wl: Shaggy two-humped camel of cold Central Asian deserts and steppes, able to drink brackish water and survive harsh winters.
crops.ch: Tame pack and riding animal for the Silk Roads; thick moulting wool; larger and calmer than its wild relatives.
crops.ce: Central Asia, probably NE Iran / Turkmenistan
crops.cn: Estimate from Bronze Age Central Asian sites, c. 3000 BCE (approximate).
crops.dn: Wikipedia: Bactrian camel domesticated c. 2500 BCE.
sp: Early domestic Bactrian camels at the Bronze Age ‘Burnt City’, c. 2500 BCE
Assyrian kings receive Bactrian camels as tribute from Median lands; the camels spread to the Near East during the 2nd millennium BCE
Camel saddles appear by c. 1200 BCE; Bactrian camels become riding and pack animals of the steppe
Caravans of Bactrian camels link China and the West
crops.today: About 2 million Bactrian camels live, almost all domestic, across the cold deserts and steppes of Central Asia, Mongolia and China.
crops.fact: The truly wild Bactrian camel of the Gobi split from the domestic camel’s ancestors some 0.7–1.1 million years ago; only about 1,000 survive.

crops.wild: Guanaco (Lama guanicoe)
crops.wl: Slender, reddish-brown wild camelid of Andean grasslands and Patagonian steppe, living in herds led by a territorial male.
crops.ch: Larger and stronger pack animal, many coat colours, coarse wool; carries 25–30 kg over mountain trails.
crops.ce: Central Andes puna, Peru (Junín; Telarmachay)
crops.cn: Shift from hunting to herding of camelids at Telarmachay and Junín c. 6,000–7,000 years ago (Wheeler).
crops.dn: Llama and alpaca domesticated at least 5,000–6,000 years ago (Wikipedia; Larson et al. 2014).
sp: The Moche bury llamas with important people and model them realistically in pottery
Llamas are the only beasts of burden of the Inca Empire
Up to 300,000 llamas haul produce from the Potosí mines (Spanish estimate)
First llamas imported to the US as zoo animals in the late 1800s; herds grow from the late 20th century
crops.today: Over 7 million llamas and alpacas lived in South America in 2007.
crops.fact: One scholar argues that Andean farming only became possible because llama dung was used as fertilizer (Chepstow-Lusty; debated).

crops.wild: Vicuña (Vicugna vicugna)
crops.wl: Small, graceful, cinnamon-coloured camelid of the high puna above 3,500 m, with extremely fine wool.
crops.ch: Larger, with much more and longer fine wool in many colours; bred for fibre rather than loads.
crops.ce: Central Andes puna, Peru (Junín; Telarmachay)
crops.cn: Shift from hunting to herding of camelids at Telarmachay and Junín c. 6,000–7,000 years ago (Wheeler).
crops.dn: Llama and alpaca domesticated at least 5,000–6,000 years ago (Wikipedia; DNA shows the vicuña as alpaca ancestor, Kadwell et al. 2001).
sp: Mummified llamas and alpacas of two breeds, c. 900–1000 years old
Alpaca wool for fine textiles of the Inca state
Charles Ledger lands 256 alpacas, llamas and vicuñas in Sydney after driving them across the Andes to Chile; the flock later dwindled
Alpacas reach North America in 1984 and are now farmed worldwide
crops.today: Over 7 million llamas and alpacas lived in South America in 2007, most alpacas in Peru.
crops.fact: After the Spanish conquest of 1532 about 98% of alpacas were destroyed; the survivors were pushed into the high Andes.

crops.wild: Montane guinea pig (Cavia tschudii)
crops.wl: Small brown, grass-eating cavy of Andean valleys and grasslands, living in groups under shrubs and rocks.
crops.ch: Larger and heavier, many coat colours and long-haired forms, calmer; bred as food and ritual animal, kept in homes.
crops.ce: Andes of southern Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia
crops.cn: Wikipedia: first domesticated as early as 5000 BC in the Andes (estimate).
crops.dn: Same estimate; selective breeding of many varieties c. 1200–1532 CE. The early date is uncertain.
sp: Ceramic-making migrants bring guinea pigs to the West Indies
Conrad Gessner describes the guinea pig, newly brought from South America
Earliest European painting of a pet guinea pig
Dutch traders bring guinea pigs to Japan
crops.today: Peruvians eat an estimated 65 million guinea pigs (cuy) each year.
crops.fact: An Elizabethan portrait of c. 1580 shows a girl holding a tortoiseshell guinea pig, only decades after Europeans first saw one.

crops.wild: Wild turkey (Meleagris gallopavo), south Mexican subspecies M. g. gallopavo
crops.wl: Large, bronze-green woodland bird of North American forests; flies short distances and roosts in trees.
crops.ch: Heavier, slower, many cannot fly or breed naturally; white feathers in most modern breeds.
crops.ce: Central and southern Mexico (Mesoamerica); a separate domestication among the Ancestral Puebloans in the US Southwest
crops.cn: Thornton et al. 2012: south-Mexican turkeys at El Mirador, Guatemala, 300 BCE–100 CE, outside their wild range.
crops.dn: Wikipedia: domesticated in Mesoamerica at least 2,000 years ago (estimate; 2,200–2,700 years in 'Domestication of animals').
sp: Mexican turkeys traded far outside their wild range, 300 BCE–100 CE
Turkeys kept for feathers, separate domestication (Speller et al. 2010)
Spaniards bring domestic turkeys from Mexico to Europe
The navigator William Strickland is credited with bringing turkeys to England; by 1573 they are Christmas fare
European domestic turkeys shipped back to North America
crops.today: About 620 million turkeys are slaughtered for meat each year.
crops.fact: Domestic turkeys descend from Mexican birds; some went to Europe and were shipped back across the Atlantic to Jamestown in 1608.

crops.wild: Wild Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata)
crops.wl: Large, black, glossy-green duck of tropical South and Central American forest rivers; perches and nests in trees.
crops.ch: Heavier, often white or pied, larger red face caruncles; quiet and tame.
crops.ce: Northern South America
crops.cn: Wikipedia 'Domestication of animals': domesticated as early as 50 CE (estimate, poorly dated).
crops.dn: Same; archaeological record is thin (estimate).
sp: Kept by many South American peoples before 1492
Brought to Europe in the 16th century; the 'Muscovy' name is unexplained
crops.today: Muscovy ducks and the mule-duck hybrids bred from them supply much of France's duck meat and foie gras.
crops.fact: Despite its name, the Muscovy duck has nothing to do with Moscow; it is one of only two birds domesticated in the Americas.

crops.wild: Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos)
crops.wl: Common wild dabbling duck of wetlands across the Northern Hemisphere; drakes have glossy green heads; strong flyers and migrants.
crops.ch: Heavier, many lay far more eggs, white or varied plumage, upright 'runner' forms; most cannot fly well.
crops.ce: Southern China (rice-paddy farmers)
crops.cn: Wikipedia: mallard domesticated in southern China around 2000 BC (estimate).
crops.dn: Same estimate.
sp: Rice farmers of southern China domesticate ducks c. 2000 BCE (few finds; date uncertain) and spread them outward
Romans keep ducks in netted pens (nessotrophia), raised from wild-caught eggs rather than bred
Pekin ducks shipped from China reach New York; Long Island becomes the centre of US duck farming
crops.today: About 4.3 billion ducks were slaughtered in 2021, over 80% of them in China.
crops.fact: In rice–duck farming in East and Southeast Asia, ducks eat pests and weeds in the paddy and manure the rice, so one field yields both.

crops.sci: Anser cygnoides domesticus and Anser anser domesticus
crops.wild: Swan goose (Anser cygnoides) in East Asia; greylag goose (Anser anser) in Europe and the Near East
crops.wl: Large grey wild geese of marshes and lakes, grazing grass in flocks and migrating in V-shaped skeins.
crops.ch: Heavier and flightless, white or pied forms; Chinese geese keep a knob on the bill; good guards and egg layers.
crops.ce: Lower Yangtze, China (Tianluoshan, Hemudu culture)
crops.cn: Eda et al. 2022 (PNAS): geese raised at Tianluoshan, Hemudu culture, c. 7,000 years ago.
crops.dn: Same; European/Egyptian greylag domestication later and less clear (debated).
sp: Geese kept in Egypt over 4,000 years ago; fully domestic by the New Kingdom
Sacred geese of Juno said to have warned Rome of the Gallic attack (legend)
Domestic geese reach Scandinavia in the Early Iron Age
crops.today: About 750 million geese are slaughtered for meat each year.
crops.fact: The domestic geese of China and of Europe come from two different wild species, yet they interbreed freely.

crops.wild: Wild yak (Bos mutus)
crops.wl: Huge black wild ox of the high Tibetan Plateau with a long shaggy skirt of hair, living above 4,000 m.
crops.ch: Smaller, often pied or white, calmer; gives milk, butter, wool and dung fuel, and carries loads at extreme altitude.
crops.ce: Tibetan Plateau (Qinghai)
crops.cn: Qiu et al. 2015: genomic estimate of domestication c. 7,300 years ago (genetic only, debated).
crops.dn: Wikipedia: oldest dated physical evidence of yak domestication c. 2,500 years ago.
crops.today: Domestic yaks live across the Himalaya, the Tibetan Plateau and the Pamirs and north into Mongolia and Siberia; their dried dung is often the only fuel on the treeless plateau.
crops.fact: Wild yak bulls can weigh a tonne, about twice as much as domestic yaks.

crops.wild: Wild reindeer / caribou (Rangifer tarandus)
crops.wl: Antlered deer of tundra and taiga, both sexes antlered; migrates in huge herds and digs lichen from under snow.
crops.ch: Only semi-domesticated: tamer, often lighter or spotted, used for milk, meat, riding and pulling sleds; still mixes with wild herds.
crops.ce: Sayan Mountains, S Siberia (rock art, proposed; debated)
crops.cn: Wikipedia: rock art suggests first domestication in the Sayan Mountains, 2–3 thousand years ago (debated).
crops.dn: Losey et al. 2021: reindeer used for draught at Ust-Polui, Yamal, c. 2,000 years ago (debated).
sp: Harness pieces and draught-worn bones of reindeer, c. 2,000 years ago (Losey et al. 2021)
Ohthere tells King Alfred he owns 600 tame reindeer
Mountain Sámi take up the semi-nomadic reindeer-herding way of life from around 1500
Reindeer brought from Siberia for Alaska Natives
crops.today: About 100,000 people herd reindeer across the circumpolar north.
crops.fact: The reindeer is the only deer semi-domesticated on a large scale, and herders still let many of their animals roam half-wild.

crops.wild: Wild colonies of the same species (honey bees were never fully domesticated)
crops.wl: Colonies of tens of thousands of bees nesting in hollow trees and rock crevices across Africa, Europe and western Asia.
crops.ch: Little genetic change: people supply hives and select calmer, productive colonies; bees still swarm and go wild easily.
crops.ce: Nile valley, Egypt (earliest hives in art)
crops.cn: Beeswax residues in Near Eastern pottery from c. 7000 BCE (Roffet-Salque et al. 2015) - exploitation, not necessarily hives.
crops.dn: Beekeeping scenes (smoke at hives) in the sun temple of Nyuserre, Egypt, before 2422 BCE.
sp: An apiary of about 100 clay hives, c. 900 BCE
Honey bees shipped to the English colony
crops.today: The world had about 83 million managed beehives in 2014 (FAO).
crops.fact: People took wild honey long before any hive: Spanish rock paintings about 8,000 years old show honey collecting.

crops.wild: Wild silk moth (Bombyx mandarina)
crops.wl: Brown moth of East Asia whose caterpillars feed on wild mulberry; adults fly well and caterpillars are camouflaged.
crops.ch: Completely dependent on people: moths are white, cannot fly, caterpillars do not wander, and cocoons are bigger.
crops.ce: Yellow River / Yangtze, China (Yangshao and Liangzhu cultures)
crops.cn: Silkworm-shaped ceramic from Nancun, Hebei, 5,400–5,500 years ago; earlier silk residues at Jiahu (c. 6500 BCE) are debated.
crops.dn: Silk fabric of domesticated silkworms at Qianshanyang, Zhejiang, c. 2700 BCE (Liangzhu); Confucian tradition also gives c. 2700 BCE.
sp: Sericulture reaches Khotan c. 50 CE (legend: a Chinese princess hid silkworms in her hair)
Monks smuggle silkworm eggs to the Byzantine Empire for Justinian I (c. 553–54)
Roger II brings Greek silk weavers to Palermo
Francis I grants Lyon’s silk weavers royal privileges; Lyon becomes Europe’s silk capital
crops.today: One cocoon yields about 900 m of silk filament.
crops.fact: The domestic silk moth cannot fly; males even need human help to find a mate, and it no longer lives in the wild.

crops.wild: European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus), originally only in Iberia and southern France
crops.wl: Small grey-brown rabbit living in colonies in burrow systems (warrens) in the dry scrub of Iberia.
crops.ch: Larger and smaller breeds, lop ears, many colours and long fur (angora); tame, breeds year-round in hutches.
crops.ce: Southern France (medieval monasteries); wild rabbits from Iberia
crops.cn: Roman authors (Varro, Pliny) describe rabbits kept in walled enclosures; captive rabbits exploited for over 2,000 years (Wikipedia).
crops.dn: Monks in southern France were crossbreeding rabbits at least by the 12th century; clear skeletal differences only from the 1800s. Gradual process (Irving-Pease et al. 2018).
sp: Romans keep rabbits in walled leporaria and spread them around the Mediterranean
Normans bring rabbits for warrens; they become established in the 12th–13th centuries (Lundy: 2,000 caught a year by 1274)
Thomas Austin releases 24 wild rabbits; they spread across the continent
Rabbits released on the mainland (Blenheim 1858, 1865) become one of the worst pests
crops.today: Rabbits are farmed for meat and fur worldwide and are among the most popular pets.
crops.fact: The tale that monks domesticated rabbits c. 600 CE because unborn rabbits counted as 'fish' at Lent is a myth (Irving-Pease et al. 2018).

crops.wild: European polecat (Mustela putorius), possibly with steppe polecat
crops.wl: Dark-brown, masked wild weasel of European woods and farmland, hunting rabbits, rodents and frogs at night.
crops.ch: Tamer, often albino or pale, depends on people; used to drive rabbits from burrows and to kill rats.
crops.ce: Mediterranean (probably Iberia / North Africa)
crops.cn: mtDNA estimate: ferrets domesticated c. 2,500 years ago (Wikipedia).
crops.dn: Same; ancient texts confirm use against rabbits by Roman times.
sp: Augustus sends ‘viverrae’ from Libya against the Balearic rabbit plague (Strabo, Pliny); possibly ferrets (debated)
An English law of 1390 restricts hunting with ferrets to the well-off
Ferrets reach the Americas in the 17th century
Ferrets imported from 1879 and some 4,000 released in 1884–86 to control rabbits; they turned to native birds
crops.today: Over five million pet ferrets live in the United States alone.
crops.fact: Ferrets were released in New Zealand to kill the introduced rabbits, and instead began eating native birds.

before.t: Fisher-hunter-gatherer camp c. 23,000 years ago: 90,000+ seeds of 100+ species; wild barley and grasses ground on a stone slab; sickle wear on flints.
Natufian hearths, 14,400 years ago: charred flatbread-like remains of wild einkorn, barley or oat flour mixed with ~50,000 club-rush tubers—4,000 years before farming.
Natufian foragers (c. 12,500–9500 BCE) gathered wild cereals, legumes, almonds, acorns and pistachios, and hunted mountain gazelle.
Foragers harvested 'wild gardens' of einkorn, emmer and rye and hunted gazelle; rye cultivation claimed from 11,050 BCE in the Younger Dryas (debated).
From c. 9500 BCE: over 7,000 grinding stones show heavy cereal processing (wild or cultivated unclear); gazelle hunted midsummer to autumn amid wild einkorn and barley.
World's oldest pottery, c. 14,500 BCE. Jōmon foragers ate chestnuts, beechnuts, acorns (tannins processed out), salmon, shellfish, sika deer and wild boar.
Camp eating seaweed (nine species, from a coast 60 km away, dated 14,220–13,980 years ago), tubers, seeds, nuts, berries and wild potato. Dating debated.
Clovis points found with Pleistocene animal bones (c. 11,500 BCE); whether Clovis people were big-game specialists or mixed foragers is disputed.
Independent farming: wetland drained by ditches about 9,000 years ago to grow taro; deliberate banana planting 6,950–6,550 years ago. UNESCO site.
